item.title: GOP chairman says WNBA response on Caitlin Clark ‘falls short,’ keeps ‘every option on the table’
item.description: Texas lawmaker August Pfluger says the WNBA's response to Congress about Caitlin Clark's treatment dodges specifics, vowing to keep every option on the table.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, chairman of the Republican Study Committee, says the WNBA’s response to congressional concerns about Caitlin Clark’s treatment "falls short" and warned that lawmakers will keep "every option on the table" as they continue pressing the league for answers.

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert responded on July 24 to a letter from Pfluger and 10 other House Republicans who questioned whether the league had adequately protected Clark and held opposing players accountable for overly physical conduct.

In the two-page response obtained exclusively by OutKick, Engelbert said the WNBA’s "top priority is the health, safety, and well-being of every player in our league, including Caitlin Clark."

REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS PRESS WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT TO PROTECT CAITLIN CLARK

In the response, the commissioner outlined the league’s standard procedures for reviewing officiating and potentially dangerous play but did not address any of the Clark-related incidents cited by the lawmakers individually.

"The WNBA’s response falls short of what we asked for, unsurprisingly," Pfluger told OutKick in a statement. "We didn’t request a description of the league’s general officiating and disciplinary procedures, we asked how those procedures have actually been applied in the specific incidents we raised involving Caitlin Clark, and the league chose not to answer that."

Engelbert wrote that WNBA Basketball Operations and Referee Operations conduct separate reviews after every game. One review examines "atypical or overly physical plays," while the other evaluates the overall performance of the officials.

WNBA MEDIA PREDICTABLY EMBARRASSES ITSELF AGAIN BY IGNORING SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM STORY OVER ALL-STAR WEEKEND

Those reviews can result in fouls being upgraded after a game, as well as fines, suspensions or other disciplinary measures. The league also uses the reviews to inform future officiating evaluations, training and guidance, Engelbert wrote.

"In all instances, the League seeks to apply the WNBA rulebook and applicable disciplinary processes consistently across all games and for all players," the commissioner said.

Pfluger said the league offered no supporting information to demonstrate that its rules had been applied evenly.

"Saying you apply your rules ‘consistently across all games and for all players’ is an assertion, not evidence, and it’s the league’s burden to show that, not ours to assume it," Pfluger said.

"Until the WNBA is willing to engage with the specifics of our information requests instead of simply restating their own policies back to us, our concerns remain unaddressed. We will continue to press for real answers and keep every option on the table until players are actually getting the protection the league claims they already provide."

Pfluger and the other lawmakers initially wrote to Engelbert on July 7, following several highly publicized incidents involving Clark. Their letter cited instances in which the Indiana Fever star had been hip-checked, poked in the eye and struck in the throat. The WNBA later assessed Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas a Flagrant Foul 2 and one-game suspension for the June 24 throat-contact incident.

The lawmakers argued that the incidents went "far beyond routine physical play" and accused the league and its officials of too often failing to address the conduct or hold opposing players accountable.

They asked Engelbert to explain the WNBA’s process for reviewing physical hostility and violence during games, how the league holds players accountable for overly aggressive actions, including conduct directed at Clark, and what it is doing to protect players from online harassment and off-court threats.

CAITLIN CLARK IS MISSING FROM ESPN'S NEW WNBA DOCUMENTARY AND THE FILMMAKERS WON'T SAY WHY

The letter also said lawmakers were concerned by reports suggesting some of Clark’s treatment could be racially motivated and warned that a failure to prevent discrimination, retaliation or a hostile work environment could raise questions under federal workplace and civil rights laws. The lawmakers requested a response by July 24.

Engelbert met the deadline, but her response did not address the alleged racial motivation, discuss any specific play involving Clark or provide comparative information about how the league’s officiating and disciplinary procedures had been applied to different players.

The response also did not say whether the WNBA conducted a separate review in response to the congressional inquiry.

Engelbert devoted part of the response to the league’s efforts to protect players from harassment away from games.

The commissioner pointed to enhanced arena and travel security, full-time charter flights, technology used to identify and report online threats, stronger fan conduct policies and expanded mental health resources. She also said the WNBA regularly communicates with teams, players and security personnel about player safety.

"The WNBA will continue its efforts to ensure all of our players are able to compete in a safe, respectful, and professional environment," Engelbert wrote.

The league’s emphasis on off-court harassment followed a July 22 joint statement from the WNBA and the Women’s National Basketball Players Association addressing an increase in racist, hateful and abusive messages directed at players.

During a July 23 interview with OutKick, conducted one day before Engelbert sent her response, Pfluger called that issue separate from the questions raised in the lawmakers’ letter.

"I’m sure there are plenty of other issues that the league needs to address, and they can do that as they see fit, but our questions are pretty pointed," Pfluger said. "The only way to clear up our questions is to actually answer them."

During the interview, Pfluger said the burden was on the WNBA to provide information demonstrating that its standards were enforced fairly. He argued that allowing a perception of unequal treatment to persist would damage confidence in the league’s ability to govern itself.

When asked during the interview to identify specific evidence supporting the original letter’s suggestion of racial motivation, Pfluger did not cite an example. He instead broadened his argument to whether every WNBA player receives equal protection under league rules.

"It is about everybody," Pfluger said. "The burden of proof should be on the commissioner, should be on the league, to provide evidence of how players on different teams and from different areas are treated."

Pfluger’s latest statement did not identify a specific congressional action he intends to pursue next, but his pledge to keep "every option on the table" leaves open the possibility of additional information requests, hearings or other scrutiny.

The WNBA did not respond to additional questions from OutKick and Fox News Digital prior to publication.

"Women’s sports are at a turning point," Pfluger said. "How the WNBA treats its own biggest star will show whether the league is actually committed to protecting the players carrying it forward."

item.title: The bedrock of American liberty was laid in Jerusalem
item.description: The City of David in biblical Jerusalem was formally recognized as an American heritage site, tracing founding ideals back three thousand years.
item.content:encoded:
When considering the sites upon which the foundations of the United States were established, Plymouth Rock, Valley Forge and Independence Hall come to mind. Yet America's Founding Fathers looked far beyond them for the inspiration to build a nation.

In October 2020, the United States formally recognized the City of David — the historic site of biblical Jerusalem — as a heritage site. Not as a Jewish heritage site, nor as an Israeli one, but as an American heritage site.

Why would the United States recognize a site more than six thousand miles beyond its borders as part of its own national heritage? Why, in 2025, would Argentina's President Javier Milei do the same, calling the City of David a source of inspiration for his republic? And why, this past week, would Guatemala become the third nation to do so?

THE WAR ON AMERICA’S JUDEO-CHRISTIAN ROOTS THREATENS EVERYTHING WE SHARE

The answer is something Americans are in danger of forgetting.

The moral bedrock on which the United States was built — and on which it endures — traces back to Jerusalem's biblical heritage. Equality before the law. Inherent human dignity. The right to speak truth to power. These revolutionary ideas didn't come from Athens, and they didn't originate in Rome. They came from Jerusalem.

Consider what they replaced: rulers who sat above the law, accountable to no one, in societies where only a select few were deemed worthy of rights at all.

RARE AMERICAN BIBLE AND FOUNDERS’ LETTERS TRACE FAITH’S ROLE IN BIRTH OF THE NATION

Yet in Jerusalem, 3,000 years ago, King David was confronted by the prophet Nathan over a moral failing, rather than execute the man who dared challenge a king, David took ownership — acknowledging his own accountability to the law, declaring that he had sinned before God and vowing to make amends.

Thomas Paine knew the source of that ideal. In Common Sense, the pamphlet that inspired the American Revolution, he pointed to the Book of Samuel and declared that in America, the law is king.

Four centuries later, in the same city, a young man named Jeremiah challenged a throne whose courts were corrupt and under which the poor were being crushed. Officials, unwilling to heed his call to change their ways, threw him into a cistern to sink in the mud and die.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

The personal seals of two of those officials — Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur, the men named in the Book of Jeremiah as plotting to put the prophet to death for the crime of speaking truth to power — were unearthed in the City of David by the archaeologist Dr. Eilat Mazar. The names in the ground match the names on the page. The First Amendment's protections of speech and dissent didn't begin in America. Their roots run back to Jerusalem.

Athens executed Socrates for asking too many questions. Jerusalem made holding truth above human power a sacred duty. Benjamin Franklin proposed seven words as the motto for the Great Seal of the United States: Rebellion to tyrants is obedience to God.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

And Thomas Jefferson wrote in the Declaration of Independence that all men are created equal, endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights.

Not endowed by the king, nor by the government. By the Creator.

The idea that every person carries inherent worth, simply by being made in the image of God, begins in Genesis — and found its first national expression in Jerusalem.

This was no secret to America's Founders. Of some 15,000 political writings of the founding era, the most-cited source was not Locke or Montesquieu. It was the Bible — cited more than both combined. They told us exactly where they got it.

These nations did not come to honor Israel and the Jewish people specifically. They came to connect themselves to Jerusalem and her story — to the ideals, rooted in this city, on which they were founded and on which they hope to endure.

In September 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood on the newly unearthed Pilgrimage Road at the City of David — the half mile that carried pilgrims from the Pool of Siloam up toward the Temple — and echoed the same sentiment: "The United States was founded… on the very powerful principle that the rights of mankind come from their Creator… But that idea did not come from the ether. It did not come from someone's imagination. It was deeply rooted in the teachings of ancient words, thousands and thousands of years old, that find their genesis here, literally on the very spot on which I stand."

As America enters her 251st year, what is the source of the ideals from which she will draw her sense of national purpose, meaning and destiny? Jerusalem offers an answer — the same inheritance it has offered for millennia, and one as relevant today as it was three thousand years ago.

item.title: King Charles sends 'defiance' message to Prince William with Buckingham Palace room offer to Harry: expert
item.description: Royal experts say Prince William demands hard boundaries with Prince Harry while King Charles seeks healing, creating a rift over the monarchy's future.
item.content:encoded:
King Charles and his heir are said to be at odds over how to handle Prince Harry.

Multiple royal experts echoed the sentiment to Fox News Digital after royal author Robert Jobson told Page Six that Prince William and his estranged brother have "different agendas" and maintain very different relationships with their father.

Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.

KING CHARLES KEPT PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON IN THE DARK ABOUT SECRET HARRY AND MEGHAN REUNION: REPORT

"When it comes to Harry, William drew a line in the sand after the publication of Harry's memoir, 'Spare,' and he is disappointed that his father is not standing up for him," Christopher Andersen, author of "The King," told Fox News Digital.

"William loves his father and appreciates better than anyone how underestimated Charles has been over the years. He wants the king to leave his mark on history. But deep down, he knows he and his family — particularly his wife, Kate — are the future of the monarchy."

WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

While Charles and William are described as being "perfectly civil to each other," sources told Page Six there are ongoing disagreements about how the monarchy should be led.

"The problem with William is that he thinks he knows best," royal biographer Hugo Vickers told the outlet.

"King Charles is tired," Andersen stressed to Fox News Digital. "He would like to have everything as it was before Megxit. But he knows how willful William is. Queen Elizabeth's cousin Margaret Rhodes told me more than once that the relationship between Charles and his late mother wasn't cozy. But what people don't know is that the royal family isn't set up to be 'cozy.' Well, it still isn't. It's 'The Firm,' remember?"

People magazine reported Harry is expected to visit his home country again in September. The Sun also reported that the king plans to offer him a room at Buckingham Palace in London for his stay. Buckingham Palace and Harry's representatives had no comment on the report when reached by People magazine.

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that Charles' reported offer to accommodate Harry in September is "a potential lifeline" that also sends a message of "defiance" to William, who reportedly wants "no further contact with his estranged brother."

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that William is known for being stubborn behind palace doors and is not one to forgive easily.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"Megxit forced William to grow up fast as the future king," she said.

"He had to protect the institution while his brother walked away. William believes the monarchy must be seen to do the right thing, even when it's painful. From what I understand, he felt his father didn't handle that firmly enough. He also believes in protecting it by drawing hard lines. But he's not the king yet."

"Where Charles may want to smooth things over, to play peacemaker with Harry, William and Catherine are determined to set boundaries. Charles is reigning, but William and Catherine are planning. And that planning is starting to look a lot like leading. Charles wants healing. William and Catherine want survival and stability. William is not doing this to be difficult. He’s doing it because he believes it’s right."

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that William and Harry have remained estranged since the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior working royals in 2020 and relocated to California. Harry and Meghan have maintained that relentless tabloid scrutiny and what they describe as a lack of support from the palace drove their decision to leave royal life.

Since stepping away from royal life, Harry and Meghan have publicly aired their grievances in high-profile interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further deepened the fallout within the royal family.

On July 10, the king hosted his younger son and his family for the first time in years in what royal observers viewed as an effort to repair the longstanding rift. The Sussexes secretly met with the king and Queen Camilla at Highgrove House, a country estate west of London, Buckingham Palace confirmed.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl reported that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware that the meeting was taking place." A source close to Charles also told Nicholl the hour-long meeting was "completely cloak-and-dagger, orchestrated by the king."

Meanwhile, William and Kate attended the DMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026 at Guards Polo Club in Windsor. The brothers did not see each other.

"Obviously, King Charles and Prince William are very different characters, sometimes with conflicting temperaments," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "What no one can alter is that William, Kate, and their family are the future of the monarchy. And it is natural for the king, who is battling cancer, to want to see his grandchildren."

Fitzwilliams argued that William made his disapproval clear on the day the king and queen saw the Sussexes by being absent from the reunion.

"William is making it clear that he has his own set of principles, his own set of rules about what is right and wrong," Andersen said.

"He feels Harry has violated those rules one too many times. It's not entirely personal. William has a strong sense of duty when it comes not only to his family but also to his country and his family's place in history. He feels Harry has shot the royal family's reputation full of holes. And for what? To become a SoCal influencer?"

"William feels Harry has betrayed not only the current generation of royals but also past generations, including their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, and future generations," Andersen added.

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that while reports of a fracture between Charles and William are overstated, the two are far from aligned on how to deal with Harry. Whether father and son can find common ground on Harry remains to be seen.

"Prince William is no fool," Fordwich said. "Every time his zero-tolerance approach is proven correct, his influence increases."

In May 2025, Harry told the BBC he would like to reconcile with his family.

"There's no point in continuing to fight anymore."
